newsitem.title: USA: GM, UAW face strike deadline at Wisconsin parts plant.
newsitem.headline: GM, UAW face strike deadline at Wisconsin parts plant.

text.p: General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers union headed toward another strike showdown Thursday, this time at a key parts plant in suburban Milwaukee that makes catalytic converters.

But in a sign of progress in the two-month old strike at GM's Pontiac, Mich., full-size pickup truck plant, bargainers talked until 10 p.m. Wednesday, about five hours longer than previous bargaining sessions.
GM spokesman Daniel Dolan said the company remains hopeful a new contract can be reached with UAW Local 1866 in Oak Creek, Wis., before the midnight Thursday strike deadline set by the union.
"We're working toward a settlement and we're hopeful we'll get something that doesn't disrupt our customers," he said.
Skip Dziedzic, president of Local 1866, could not be reached Thursday but said late Wednesday there had been minimal progress in negotiations.

The two sides are at odds over staffing levels, health and safety issues, long-term job security and subcontracting, a practice also known as outsourcing, which the union has been battling GM on for months.

The approximately 900 hourly workers at the plant make catalytic converters for GM's Delphi Energy and Engine Management Systems unit. The plant supplies parts to most of GM's North American assembly operations, as well as customers in Europe in Asia.
GM faces two other strike deadlines Friday, June 13, at a foundry in Saginaw, Mich., and a metal stamping facility in Grand Rapids, Mich.

David Cole, director of the University of Michigan's Study for the Centre of Automotive Transportation, said he believes both sides want to clean up long-simmering local contracts before the two-week summer shutdown that starts in July.
"I don't think we're going to see any major disruptions," he said. "The intent is to get these things done soon, by the first of July."
As of last week, about 20 of GM's more than 100 UAW locals did not have local pacts. A new three-year national agreement was signed and ratified last fall.
In Pontiac, about 5,700 members from UAW Local 594 have been on strike since April 22 in a dispute over staffing levels, health and safety issues and other grievences.
One analyst, who did not want to be named, said GM may blame any delays in the May 1998 production launch of its next generation of full-size pickup trucks on the strike.

GM spokesman Dan Flores said the strike has not adversely affected the timing or development of future vehicle programmes. However, he acknowledged that about 1,300 of those on strike do normally work in engineering, design, testing and lab facilities for new products at the Pontiac complex.

The University of Michigan's Cole said the softening of full-size pickup truck sales is likely causing GM to question how much capacity it will need in the future. Including Pontiac East, GM has five plants that make full-size pickups and sport/utility vehicles.
"It's conceivable the whole Pontiac plant could be at risk now because they may not need as many plants," he said.
GM said last month that a two-month strike in Oklahoma, City, Okla., and the Pontiac work stoppage have cost it $225 million in lost profits.
So far this year, GM has been hit with five strikes -- three by the UAW and two by the International Brotherhood of Electronic Workers. Last year, GM lost $1.2 billion in income due to strikes.
GM's stock lost 50 cents to end at $57 on the New York Stock Exchange.
